raw_case_text:
An 18-months-old male child presented with history of high-grade fever for 1 month, cough for 15 days and progressive breathlessness of 7 days duration without relief of symptoms by medications prescribed by a local medical practitioner. History of loose stools, vomiting, significant weight loss, and contact with tuberculosis were absent. He belonged to a low socioeconomic class. He was a predominantly breast fed baby, and his mother had been suffering from fever 2 months back, which responded to 10 days of antibiotic therapy.
On examination, it was seen that he was acutely ill, irritable, pale, and febrile (temperature 39  C). His weight was 9.6 kg. (> -2 SD as per WHO growth charts); the heart rate was 130/min; respiratory rate was 60/min with intercostal recession along with diminished air entry on the left side. Liver and spleen were not palpable. Diagnosis of left-sided pleural effusion was made and the same was confirmed on chest x-ray [Figure 1a]. Ultrasonography (USG) and CT further confirmed left-sided pleural effusion. Pleural tap was done and 150 mL of viscid purulent fluid was aspirated.
Cell count of pleural fluid revealed a total of 6800 cells/mm3 (84% polymorphs and 16% lymphocytes) and proteins of 4.6 gm/dL. Intercostal drain (ICD) was placed and intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin was started empirically. Gram stain of pleural fluid revealed Gram negative bacilli. After 48 hrs of incubation, culture growth obtained was subjected to biochemical testes. These tests were suggestive of S. typhi. The organism was further confirmed using serotyping method and the confirmed S. typhi was reported along with antibiogram. Antibiogram showed sensitivity to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, amikacin, ofloxacin, and ciprofloxacin. Ceftriaxone alone was continued. Blood and stool cultures were sterile and Widal test was positive (O titer of 1:120 and H titer of 1:240). Hemoglobin was 8.8 gm% and total leucocyte counts was 20,500 (Polymorphs 78%, Lymphocytes 20%, Eosinophils 2%,). Peripheral smear examination showed normocytic normochromic anemia with reticulocyte count of 2%. Liver function tests, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, iron profile, sickling test, and ultrasound abdomen were normal.
Intercostal drainage tube was removed after 5 days when no drainage was seen from the tube. However, even after 10 days of antibiotic therapy fever was persisting and x-ray chest was still hazy; therefore, a CT thorax was done that revealed loculated pus in the left pleural cavity [Figure 1b]. Based on pleural fluid culture sensitivity report, ofloxacin was added to the treatment. After 6 days of further treatment, the patient became afebrile and chest X-ray improved markedly with a total of fourteen days of ofloxacin therapy [Figure 2]. Repeat USG revealed minimal pleural effusion less than 30 cc. ELISA for HIV of both child and mother were negative and immunoglobulin profile (IgG, IgA, and IgM) of the child were normal. Echocardiography done to rule out pericardial involvement was normal. The patient was doing well during a year's follow up. To find out the source of infection in this child we investigated his mother, and performed cultures of her blood, urine, stool, and breast milk. Mother's stool culture was positive for S. typhi, and other cultures were sterile. A course of amoxicillin was prescribed for treatment of her carrier status and repeat stool culture after a month of follow up was sterile.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-month-old male infant presented with a 1-month history of high-grade fever, 15 days of cough, and 7 days of progressive breathlessness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child developed high-grade fever for 1 month, cough for 15 days, and progressive breathlessness over the preceding 7 days that failed to improve with outpatient medications prescribed by a local practitioner.
subjective.past_medical_history: Predominantly breastfed infant from a low socioeconomic background. His mother had a febrile illness 2 months prior that resolved after 10 days of antibiotic therapy. No known contact with tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, cough, and progressive dyspnea. Pertinent negatives: no loose stools, vomiting, or significant weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the child was acutely ill, irritable, pale, and febrile (temperature 39 °C), weighing 9.6 kg (>-2 SD per WHO growth charts). Heart rate was 130/min, and respiratory rate was 60/min with intercostal recessions and diminished air entry over the left hemithorax. The liver and spleen were not palpable.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 8.8 g%, total leukocyte count 20,500/mm^3 (polymorphs 78%, lymphocytes 20%, eosinophils 2%), and peripheral smear showing normocytic normochromic anemia with 2% reticulocytes. Liver function tests, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, iron profile, sickling test, abdominal ultrasound, and echocardiography were normal. HIV ELISA (child and mother) and child serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) were normal. Blood and stool cultures of the child were sterile, while Widal test was positive (O titer 1:120, H titer 1:240). Chest X-ray and chest ultrasonography confirmed a left-sided pleural effusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracentesis aspirated 150 mL of viscid purulent pleural fluid with 6,800 cells/mm^3 (84% polymorphs, 16% lymphocytes) and protein 4.6 g/dL; Gram stain showed Gram-negative bacilli, and culture with biochemical testing and serotyping confirmed Salmonella typhi sensitive to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, amikacin, ofloxacin, and ciprofloxacin. Because fever and chest X-ray haziness persisted at day 10 (5 days after chest tube removal), a thoracic CT was performed and demonstrated loculated pus in the left pleural cavity. Maternal epidemiological workup (blood, urine, stool, and breast milk cultures) isolated S. typhi from the mother's stool culture.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Left-sided Salmonella typhi pleural empyema in an immunocompetent infant transmitted from an asymptomatic maternal fecal carrier, confirmed by pleural fluid culture/serotyping and positive Widal test (O 1:120, H 1:240), with maternal stool culture positive for S. typhi. HIV, immunodeficiency, sickle cell disease, and pericardial involvement were ruled out. Initial management with intercostal tube drainage (removed after 5 days) and empiric IV ceftriaxone plus vancomycin (narrowed to ceftriaxone alone) left residual loculated empyema and persistent fever on day 10. Guided by pleural fluid susceptibility testing, ofloxacin was added for 14 days, achieving defervescence within 6 days and marked radiological clearance (<30 mL residual fluid on repeat ultrasound). The child remained well at 1-year follow-up, and the mother was successfully eradicated of her S. typhi carrier state with a course of amoxicillin (sterile repeat stool culture at 1 month).
